paper_title: Co-Evolution in Agentic Systems: Toward Self-Directed Evolution Beyond Human Design

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic systems are increasingly expected to improve after deployment, yet single-entity self-evolution is often bounded by a static learning context, such as fixed tasks and feedback. This survey focuses on co-evolution in agentic systems, a multi-component form of self-evolution in which multiple agents and their environment impose adaptive pressure on one another. To organize existing papers, we propose a progressive three-stage taxonomy that traces how the system gradually sheds human-engineered constraints. Agent--Agent Co-Evolution studies how agents adapt through dynamic peers, including adversarial, collaborative, and organizational adaptation. Agent--Environment Co-Evolution extends this loop to adaptive tasks, feedback, and interaction spaces that change with the agents. Meta Co-Evolution further explores the possibility of making the evolution mechanism itself evolvable. We also discuss open challenges in evaluating such systems, scaling them across multiple components, and keeping increasingly autonomous evolutionary processes safe and controllable. This survey provides a unified foundation for building robust and open-ended agentic systems that can improve beyond fixed human-designed paths.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in AI have shifted attention from isolated models to agentic systems, which can autonomously interact with other agents and external environments (Guo et al., 2024; Plaat et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). They may be augmented with harness (Ning et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026b), including tools (Xu et al., 2025b), memory (Du, 2026), and skills (Zhou et al., 2026). As agentic systems become increasingly complex, central question is how they can continue to improve after deployment (Gao et al., 2026). Self-evolution is major paradigm for continual improvement in agentic systems, where an Figure 1: Comparison between single-entity selfevolution and multi-component co-evolution. agent persistently updates itself from experience, feedback, and failures without human intervention. One important form is single-entity selfevolution, where updates occur within one agent, such as refining its model backbone (Zhai et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025), updating memory (Suzgun et al., 2026), or improving skills (Xiao et al., 2026). However, it can remain bounded by fixed external conditions, as illustrated in Figure 1. This limitation echoes the Red Queen effect (Van Valen, 2014): sustained progress requires mutual adaptation rather than adaptation on only one side. Co-evolution extends self-evolution by making the counterpart adaptive (Hillis, 1990). In agentic systems, agents may evolve with adaptive peers such as opponents or collaborators (Pan et al., 2026b), or with environments such as tasks, feedback, and interaction spaces (Guo et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026h). Recent work further suggests meta-level extension in which the evolution mechanism itself becomes evolvable (Iacob et al., 2026). Across these settings, multiple components jointly adapt and continually reshape each others further evolution, rather than merely exchanging information or interacting. Despite growing interest, no survey has centered Figure 2: The progressive taxonomy of co-evolution, which reflects an expanding boundary of evolutionary freedom. on such co-evolutionary agentic systems. They examine LLM-based agents and multi-agent systems (Guo et al., 2024; Plaat et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025), agent components and harness engineering (Xu et al., 2025b; Du, 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026), and environment scaling for interactive agents (Huang et al., 2025c). Surveys on self-evolving agents (Gao et al., 2026; Xiang et al., 2026) are closest to our scope, but treat coevolution as subtheme rather than the central organizing axis. We address this gap by asking which components co-evolve, how the boundary of evolutionary freedom expands across components, and what the ultimate form of this process might be. To organize this literature, we propose progressive three-stage taxonomy structured by the expanding scope of what system is allowed to evolve, tracing how system gradually sheds human-engineered constraints. (1) AgentAgent Co-Evolution captures mutual adaptation among evolving peers within fixed environment, including changes to their model backbones, harness components, and organizational structures. (2) AgentEnvironment Co-Evolution extends adaptation to environmental components, including tasks, feedback, and interaction spaces. (3) Meta Co-Evolution captures an emerging stage in which the evolution mechanism itself becomes adaptive, allowing the system to revise what, when, how, and where to evolve, as well as how to evaluate. This progression expands evolutionary freedom from agents alone, to agents and environments, and ultimately to the rules governing their evolution, providing possible pathway toward open-endedness (Stanley et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2024), where systems keep improving rather than converging to fixed endpoint. This survey makes three contributions. (1) to our knowledge, we offer the first focused survey of co-evolution in agentic systems, distinguishing mutual adaptation from mere interaction or (2) we organize the litinformation exchange. erature with progressive three-stage taxonomy that traces how evolutionary freedom expands from agents alone, to agents and environments, and ultimately to an evolvable evolution mechanism. (3) we discuss open challenges and future directions for evaluating, scaling, and governing increasingly autonomous co-evolutionary systems. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. 2 defines formal foundations and introduces our three-stage progressive taxonomy. 35 review methods across the three stages. 6 discusses challenges and future directions. 7 concludes.

sections.title: 2.1 What Is an Agentic System?
sections.content: An agentic system = (A, E) consists of an agent collective and an environment E. An agent is system unit that can autonomously interact with other agents or the environment. To track evolution, we treat each agent as unified evolving unit and denote it by ai = (mi, hi): model backbone mi and harness hi (Yao et al., 2026b), such as memory, tools, skills, prompts, or workflows. In practice, hi may include only some of these components, or none. Agents may share the same backbone yet remain distinct if their harnesses instantiate different roles or objectives. An agent evolves when either component changes: ai = 0 (mi = 0) (hi = 0). Agents are not an unordered set. They are structured by Π, which encodes their roles, communication topology, and division of labor: = (cid:0){a1, . . . , an}, Π(cid:1). evolves whenever an ai or Π changes. The environment is everything external to that agents act upon and receive feedback from. trajectory τ records the sequence of thought actionobservation cycles (Yao et al., 2023) accumulated by the system up to step t.

sections.title: 2.3 Three-Stage Taxonomy
sections.content: Our three-stage taxonomy (Figure 2) follows the expanding scope of what system is allowed to evolve. From one stage to the next, humanengineered constraints are gradually removed. Stage 1 AgentAgent Co-Evolution. Coevolution begins when an agent no longer learns against static counterpart. As agents respond to one another, each agents progress changes the challenges and opportunities facing its peers, and the collective may also reorganize its structure Π. This creates coupled evolutionary process within the agent collective: i=1, Πt+1(cid:1) = Ω(At, E, τ t). At+1 = (cid:0){at+1 }n Stage 2 AgentEnvironment Co-Evolution. This coupled process can continuously change the agents, but not the environment in which they interact. When the environment remains fixed, it limits the new experiences and pressures that the agents can encounter. Stage 2 therefore extends the process to the environment itself, allowing agent behavior to reshape the whole conditions that subsequently shape the agents: (At+1, Et+1) = Ω(At, Et, τ t). Stage 3 Meta Co-Evolution. In Stage 2, the evolution mechanism remains human-designed, so the system can change its contents but not how they change. We therefore define meta co-evolution as stage where the lower-level co-evolving system further revises its evolution mechanism through self-generated revision process Γt: Ωt+1 = Γt(St, Ωt, τ t), St+1 = Ωt+1(St, τ t). This recursion provides pathway toward openendedness (Stanley et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2024), where the system continues to generate meaningful novelty rather than converging to fixed endpoint, characterized by continuous novelty, Ωt+1 = Ωt, and unbounded divergence, with adaptive capability satisfying limt H(St, Ωt) = .

sections.title: 3 Agent–Agent Co-Evolution
sections.content: This stage studies co-evolution within the agent collective = ({ai}n i=1, Π), where each agents main source of improvement is the other evolving agents around it. We organize this stage into three patterns: adversarial and collaborative co-evolution distinguished by agents goal relations, and evolving agent organizations that further adapt agents roles and interaction structures.

sections.title: 3.1 Adversarial Agents
sections.content: Adversarial agents co-evolve through opposing objectives, where each side is rewarded for defeating the other, so one agents progress directly raises the difficulty its opponent faces. We organize this literature by how the pressure scales, from pairwise pressure between two evolving sides to multisource pressure across many adversarial agents.

sections.title:
3.1.1 Pairwise Adversarial Pressure
This co-evolution arises between two adversarial
agents with distinct roles, and can trace back to the
GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014), where a generator
produces fake images and a discriminator learns to
tell them from real ones, each improving with the
other. The same idea was soon used for embodied
control. RARL (Pinto et al., 2017) trains a control
policy against an adversary that adds destabiliz-
ing forces, making it robust to real disturbances
rather than a fixed noise pattern. Through competi-
tive self-play in fighting games (Bansal et al., 2018)
and hide-and-seek (Baker et al., 2020), agents learn
tool use and counter-strategies as they escalate
against each other. The idea later moved to lan-
guage, where SPAG (Cheng et al., 2024) trains
both agents of a word-guessing game, with one
sections.content: Figure 3: Paper landscape of co-evolution in agentic systems. trying to make the other say secret word while the other tries to guess it. Most recently, this idea has been widely applied to LLM safety, where an attacker agent generates jailbreak prompts and defender agent learns to refuse them, each driving the other to improve. ACE-Safety (Li et al., 2025c) searches for attacks with Monte Carlo tree search, AdvGRPO (Bullwinkel et al., 2026) stabilizes joint GRPO with dense multi-channel rewards, and Yun et al. (2025) makes already-found attacks stop working, so the attacker keeps discovering new attack types instead of collapsing to few modes. MAGIC (Wen et al., 2026) runs multi-turn game, so the attacker can find weaknesses that single-turn attacks cannot, and CHASE (Markasserithodi et al., 2026) drops preset attack templates so its defender stays robust to unseen attacks. Some works also merge both roles into one model through self-play, where Self-RedTeam (Liu et al., 2025) keeps both online against each other and Wang et al. (2026a) replays past failures to avoid forgetting hard cases. Beyond direct prompts, ARLAS (Wang et al., 2025c) extends the game to tool use, hiding harmful instructions in the tool outputs an agent reads.

sections.title: 3.1.2 Multi-Source Adversarial Pressure
sections.content: Multi-source adversarial pressure arises when an agent must remain competitive against multiple opponents. AlphaStar (Vinyals et al., 2019) provides classical example through league training in real-time strategy game, main agents co-evolve with exploiters that target their weaknesses and past versions that prevent forgetting. Later works extend this idea in different ways. Ma et al. (2024a) co-evolve defender against diverse population of red-team models, so it generalizes across attack styles instead of overfitting to single attacker. TriPlay-RL (Tan et al., 2026) coevolves three agents, an attacker, defender, and an evaluator, so that attack generation, safe response, and safety judgment evolve together. AdvEvoMARL (Pan et al., 2025) trains attackers against whole team of task agents, which learn to resist attacks while doing their jobs, so safety is built into the group rather than separate guard.

sections.title: 3.2 Collaborative Agents
sections.content: Unlike adversarial agents, collaborative agents coevolve through shared goals, where one agents improvement forces its partners to adjust what they coordinate with and build on. We distinguish two structures, parallel collaboration, where equivalent agents either have no roles or can take any role, and role-differentiated collaboration, where fixed and distinct roles give agents different paths of improvement.

sections.title:
3.2.1 Parallel Collaboration
Parallel collaboration originates in Multi-Agent Re-
inforcement Learning (MARL), where peer agents
share a single task reward and co-adapt as the
others chang (Lowe et al., 2017; Foerster et al.,
2018; Yang et al., 2018). Recent work brings this
to LLM agents. Liu et al. (2026f) trains them
with shared rewards and group-relative advantages,
while Liu et al. (2026e) compares joint-history and
sections.content: local-history critics to stabilize their co-evolution. MARS2 (Li et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b) lets multiple agents co-evolve on shared search tree, spreading each programs test reward across the tree instead of only its final node. Beyond the final outcome, other work draws coevolutionary pressure from the collaboration process itself (Omidshafiei et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2020). Some methods turn interaction traces into rewards, where CoMAS (Xue et al., 2025) and MAPoRL (Park et al., 2025) reward agents from their discussion, such as whether turn corrects or persuades later responses. Others revise the signals that guide later cooperation, where LIET (Li et al., 2025b) builds shared cooperation-tip list from messages, M3HF (Wang et al., 2025b) converts feedback on team behavior into per-agent rewards, and MAC-SPGG (Liang et al., 2025) uses sequential public-goods reward to discourage free-riding. Parallel collaboration can also span separate workspaces, where agents explore independently and share what they learn, as in CORAL (Qu et al., 2026), which diffuses attempts, notes, and skills through shared memory, and GEA (Weng et al., 2026), which treats the group as the evolutionary unit so that execution logs, failures, and improvement from one agent guide the updates of others.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Role-Differentiated Collaboration
sections.content: Role-differentiated collaboration co-evolves agents with distinct roles. common pattern is produceand-revise loop. CORY (Ma et al., 2024b) is minimal form where pioneer answers and an observer revises, with periodic role exchange keeping the two coupled. RL Tango (Zha et al., 2025) trains the verifier from outcome correctness to give process feedback, while CoVerRL (Pan et al., 2026b) bootstraps its verifier from majority-vote answers when labels are unavailable. WaltzRL (Zhang et al., 2025b) jointly trains conversation agent and critique agent, rewarding it only when its suggestions improve the partners next response. Others split tasks by agent capability. EvoScientist (Lyu et al., 2026) lets researcher and engineer agents accumulate experience across tasks through persistent memories. SiriuS (Zhao et al., 2025) trains domain agents such as physicist, mathematician, and summarizer from successful and repaired collaboration trajectories, while MARS (Chen et al., 2026a) couples System1 information compression with System2 reasoning through shared trajectory rewards. Finally, MARFT (Liao et al., 2025) and Stronger-MAS (Zhao et al., 2026) focus on credit assignment, attributing the shared team reward to each role so every role can improve.

sections.title: 3.3 Evolving Agent Organizations
sections.content: Beyond fixed roles, agents can co-evolve with the organization, including role assignments and interaction structure. R3DM (Goel et al., 2025) discovers roles from agent behavior and co-adapts them with agent policies, pushing agents toward distinct behaviors. SkillMAS (Pan et al., 2026a) jointly updates agent skills and team structure, restructuring it when execution traces reveal mismatch. MetaAgent-X (Zhang et al., 2026c) trains the workflow designer and executor agents together so they improve each other.

sections.title: 4 Agent–Environment Co-Evolution
sections.content: This stage studies co-evolution between agents and an adaptive environment E. As agents improve, the environment reshapes the tasks they face, the feedback on their outputs, or the worlds they act in, and we classify methods by which change primarily drives further agent evolution.

sections.title: 4.1 Task-Space Co-Evolution
sections.content: In task-space co-evolution, the environment adapts what problem the agent solves next. This literature takes two forms, selecting tasks from an existing pool and generating new task specifications.

sections.title:
4.1.1 Exposure and Selection
Exposure and selection methods keep the task
space fixed and adapt which tasks the agent sees.
Early work adjusted exposure by learning progress.
For discrete tasks or data sources, curriculum learn-
ing (Matiisen et al., 2020) adjusts sampling weights
by estimated progress, while methods over continu-
ous task parameters (Klink et al., 2019, 2020; Porte-
las et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2021) steer sampling
toward the agent’s current competence, an idea Xu
et al. (2025a) later extends with a teacher model
that raises the sampling of tasks the student still
fails. Beyond competence matching, replay-based
selection (Jiang et al., 2021b,a) revisits past levels
that still offer learning potential, and regret-based
selection (Beukman et al., 2024; Monette et al.,
2025) prioritizes configurations where the agent
lags behind a stronger reference. In multi-agent
settings, Bhati et al. (2023) control task difficulty
through changing the exposure to teammates with
different capabilities. PORTAL (Wu et al., 2024)
sections.content: selects intermediate tasks that lead agents to hard target step by step. For LLM agents, Wang et al. (2026c) resamples tasks matching the agents own failure modes, and SEAD (Dai et al., 2026) samples simulated user profiles that become harder for the service agent to handle as it improves.

sections.title: 4.1.2 Adaptive Task Generation
sections.content: Generative task construction creates new tasks rather than reshuffling an existing pool, placing them near the agents current competence frontier (Florensa et al., 2018). Even when task is produced by an agent, it belongs to environment evolution, because that agent is not peer competing or collaborating within the same task. Embodied work makes this explicit through goal generation. OpenAI et al. (2021) explores environment for challenging yet reachable goals, and Kharyal et al. (2025) broaden goal coverage with multiple teachers. CCL (Lin et al., 2025) extends this to multi-agent RL with agent-specific subtasks. Recent LLM-agent methods instantiate this loop across several interactive settings. In tool use, generators calibrate task difficulty to the solvers success rate (Guo et al., 2025; Acikgoz et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a), convert its failed rollouts into new tasks (Wang et al., 2026e; Yang et al., 2026; Zhai et al., 2025b), or pair each task with verification function (Zhou et al., 2025). In search tasks, proposers generate multi-hop verifiable questions from retrieval behavior (Lu et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025b; Yue et al., 2026). In GUI and computer-use, some methods explore unfamiliar software to learn what operations it supports and turn these into tasks (Liu et al., 2026a; Xue et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2025c), others derive tasks from the agents failed attempts (Qi et al., 2025) or by perturbing parameters such as time and quantity in existing tasks (Lin et al., 2026), and others (Xue et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026) generate the validators and setup scripts that each task needs to run. In software engineering, Socratic-SWE (Xiao et al., 2026) builds repository repair tasks from its solving traces. Finally, RLAnything (Wang et al., 2026d) jointly rewrites tasks, policy, and reward across computer-use, game, and coding tasks.

sections.title: 4.2 Feedback-Space Co-Evolution
sections.content: Beyond adapting what tasks agents face, the environment can also co-evolve in how it evaluates, rewards, or diagnoses agent behavior.

sections.title: 4.2.1 Preference-Driven Feedback
sections.content: Feedback co-evolution may be driven by an evolving reward model that learns from preference comparisons (Christiano et al., 2017) over trajectory pairs, scored by scripted teacher rather than human. PEBBLE (Lee et al., 2021) relabels replaybuffer trajectories whenever the reward model changes, reusing stored rollouts instead of collecting fresh labels. To further cut labeling, Liang et al. (2022) and Zhu et al. (2025b) seek pairs where the reward model is least confident, DAPPER (Kadokawa et al., 2026) pairs trajectories from different policies to widen behavioral contrast, and DUO (Feng et al., 2025) targets pairs with strong reward disagreement and diverse segment behavior.

sections.title: 4.2.2 Outcome-Driven Feedback
sections.content: Feedback co-evolution may also be driven by task outcomes. In embodied control (Song et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024c; Sun et al., 2025a; Hazra et al., 2025), LLM-based systems train policy under candidate reward function and revise that function from trajectory returns or task failures. ROSKA (Huang et al., 2025a) and LaRes (Li et al., 2026b) co-search reward candidates and policy variants, keeping the best-performing rewards, REGoT (Yao et al., 2026a) refines decomposed rewards from rollout feedback including visual evaluation, and Lu et al. (2025c) updates reward parameters from policy regret. CURE (Wang et al., 2025a) and CoEvoSkills (Zhang et al., 2026a) evolve their unit tests or surrogate verifiers from execution failures. Beyond rewriting rewards or verifiers, Lu et al. (2026b) adds corrective hints early in training, then withdraws them as the agent improves, while AHRS (Huang et al., 2025b) reweights fixed reward terms by their current contribution to learning.

sections.title: 4.2.3 Consistency-Augmented Feedback
sections.content: Consistency constraints further augment evaluator learning on top of preference or outcome signals. SURF (Park et al., 2022) augments sparse labels by reusing segment pairs the reward model already ranks confidently. R* (Li et al., 2025a) updates reward parameters only when several critics agree on the same segment ranking. ARCO (Tian et al., 2026) co-trains step-scoring rubric evaluator with the policy and requires those step scores to add up to the final task outcome. NLAC (Hong et al., 2025) trains language critic so that its predictions of what comes next stay consistent with later steps on the trajectory, and ECHO (Li et al., 2026c) updates Figure 4: Cross-paper evidence for the effect, consistency, and convergence of co-evolution. See Appendix for data selection and aggregation details. its diagnostic critic only when acting on its advice actually improves the policy. 4.3 Interaction-Space Co-Evolution Beyond tasks and feedback, the environment can also adapt where the agent acts in, either constructing an increasingly challenging executable world or learning world model to replace the real one.

sections.title: 4.3.1 Executable World Construction
sections.content: In classical gridworld navigation and continuous control, POET (Wang et al., 2019) evolves population of environment-agent pairs, while regretbased methods (Dennis et al., 2020; Parker-Holder et al., 2022; Chung et al., 2024) generate levels that target the agents weaknesses. More recently, DEGen (Mead et al., 2025) generates level parts online as the student explores, and COvolve (Sygkounas et al., 2026) uses an LLM to co-evolve the code for both levels and agent controllers. In robotics and embodied simulation, ADR (OpenAI et al., 2019) widens simulation randomization as the policy improves, while later work generates worlds directly. OMNI-EPIC (Faldor et al., 2025) filters new environments by interestingness, and LLM-POET (Aki et al., 2024) adapts POET to embodied simulation with an LLM generator, Others (Liang et al., 2024; Abouelazm et al., 2025; Yeo et al., 2026) generate environments whose difficulty tracks the agents learning potential, and SimWorld Studio (Kang et al., 2026) builds 3D scenes validated by physics and vision checks. In games and open-ended worlds, XLand (Team et al., 2021) adapts game rules and layouts to agent performance. MAESTRO (Samvelyan et al., 2023) extends regret-based design to multi-agent games by generating levels around different co-players. EnvGen (Zala et al., 2024) regenerates environments targeting the agents weak skills, and DiCode (Mitsides et al., 2026) grows level archive, generating new levels from the highest-value ones. For tool-use agents, Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026) expands tool combinations and database states to expose new capability gaps, while SEAL (Hu et al., 2026) refines the environments constraints and recovery feedback from verified rollouts to correct recurring agent errors. Finally, construction targets the rules governing agent populations. Zheng et al. (2020) learns tax policy that reshapes the incentives of economic agents, and Li et al. (2024) evolve social norms that reshape agent behavior across generations.

sections.title: 4.3.2 Model-Based World Construction
sections.content: Recent work replaces real environments with world models that co-evolve with agents. In text-based settings, WebEvolver (Fang et al., 2025b) co-trains web world model with the agent policy as virtual web server for synthetic rollouts and look-ahead. COMAP (Liu et al., 2026h) uses an on-policy textual world model to predict future feedback that guides action refinement. DreamGym (Chen et al., 2025b) synthesizes transitions from an experience model whose replay buffer grows during training. PaW (Lu et al., 2026a) adds next observation prediction as an auxiliary signal in agent RL. In role-play simulation, EvolvingWorld (Zong et al., 2026) lets the world model decide which aspects to track and evolves the world state that later shapes character evolution. In embodied and visual domains, world models reduce costly real-world interaction. EvolvingAgent (Feng et al., 2026) improves world model and agent planner from Minecraft experience. Liu et al. (2026g) and Guo et al. (2026) use video world model predicting future frames to train the agent policy, and the two improve together. LCDrive (Tan et al., 2025) optimizes latent world-model tokens together with driving actions through closed-loop RL.

sections.title: 5.1 Toward Open-Endedness
sections.content: As shown in Figure 4, Stage 1 and Stage 2 improve performance across most settings, but the gains become smaller as evolution approaches plateau. By allowing the evolution mechanism to change, meta co-evolution may move beyond this bottleneck and open new directions for improvement. Meta co-evolution offers route toward openendedness (Stanley et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2024), which requires continuous novelty (Ωt+1 = Ωt), so mechanism updates can keep opening new learnable directions, and unbounded divergence (limt H(St, Ωt) = ), so the systems adaptive capacity has no finite upper bound. In this sense, meta co-evolution is not merely another category, but step from adaptation under designed rules toward self-expanding agentic systems. We decompose the evolution mechanism into five adaptive decisions: (1) what to evolve selects the adaptation target, such as an agent backbone, harness, or organization, or environment artifacts like tasks, rewards, and worlds; (2) when to evolve triggers updates after failures, plateaus, or distribution shifts; (3) how to evolve produces variants through backbone training, harness revision, or structural generation and editing; (4) where to evolve covers both the domain of evolution, such as tool use, web, or robotics, and the setting it runs in, such as sandboxes, simulated or real environments; and (5) how to evaluate judges evolution quality by performance, novelty, safety, or robustness, shaping the direction of later evolution. This criterion separates meta co-evolution from isolated meta-evolution. The mechanism revision must be induced by the joint trajectory of lower-level coevolving ecosystem and must then alter that ecosystems subsequent evolutionary conditions.

sections.title: 5.2 From Precursors to Meta Co-Evolution
sections.content: Most related methods remain single-entity precursors. PromptBreeder (Fernando et al., 2024) evolves mutation prompts that control how future task prompts change. Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2025) and HyperAgents (Zhang et al., 2026b) evolve the agents own self-modification machinery. MemEvolve (Zhang et al., 2025a) evolves the memory architecture that governs experience reuse, while SIA (Hebbar et al., 2026) uses trajectory feedback to choose between harness and weight updates. These methods make the evolution mechanism evolvable but lack lower-level co-evolving system. RQGM (Iacob et al., 2026) goes beyond by coevolving task agents and evaluators, while its metaagent uses joint feedback to guide later evolution.

sections.title: 6 Challenges and Future Directions
sections.content: evaluation. Existing benchmarks Dynamic mainly measure an agents final capabilities across domains such as tool use (Yao et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2026b,c,d), web browsing (Zhou et al., 2024a; Wei et al., 2025), software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024; Miserendino et al., 2025), computer use (Trivedi et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Merrill et al., 2026), and multi-agent interaction (Zhou et al., 2024b; Mou et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025a). PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) takes step toward evolution-aware evaluation by testing whether an agent can autonomously post-train base LLM. However, evaluating co-evolution requires going further: it must determine whether all evolving components improve, whether their gains transfer to unseen partners and environments, and how each component contributes to the joint progress. Since higher task success can hide exploitative behavior (Thaman, 2026), such systems may fail through evaluator exploitation, partner overfitting, or diversity collapse. Evaluation should therefore pair fixed benchmarks with process-level testing, such as historical cross-play, component ablations, and held-out evaluators. Scaling co-evolution. Current systems mostly study local loops, such as attackerdefender training (Wen et al., 2026), policyreward adaptation (Lu et al., 2025c), or agenttask generation (Acikgoz et al., 2026). Future work can scale these to systems where agents, their harness, and the environment all change together. The challenge is not to make more components adaptive, but to decide which should change, how their updates influence one another, and how to keep the co-evolution pressure productive rather than unstable or dominated by one component. Meta co-evolution begins to address this challenge by letting the system make these evolutionary decisions itself, moving beyond human-predefined paths of improvement. Safety and governance. As co-evolution becomes more autonomous, humans may lose control over the systems behavior. Evolving agents may develop attack strategies, tool-use patterns, communication protocols (Tucker et al., 2022; Motwani et al., 2024), or organizational behaviors that exceed human understanding and are hard to monitor. The risk is sharper in meta co-evolution, where systems may also alter which behaviors are rewarded and preserved. Future work therefore needs governance that keeps open-ended evolution auditable and interruptible, including sandboxed deployment, continuous monitoring, rollback to verified states, and human intervention points.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: This survey focuses on co-evolution in agentic systems, where multiple components impose evolutionary pressure on one another. We organize the field through progressive taxonomy whose adaptive boundary expands from agents alone, to agents together with their environments, and finally to the mechanism governing their joint evolution, reflecting gradual reduction of human intervention. This perspective shows that future progress lies not in stronger static agents but in agents that continually improve through co-evolution, supported by evaluation and governance that keep the process reliable and controllable.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Meta co-evolution is still at an early stage. Only limited work currently meets our definition of Stage 3. Much of our discussion therefore draws on single-entity meta-evolution as precursor, which shows that evolution mechanisms can themselves evolve but does not couple this change to lowerlevel co-evolving system. Safety and governance are not operationalized. We identify safety, monitoring, and human oversight as first-order concerns for increasingly autonomous co-evolution, and point to failure modes specific to co-evolving systems, such as evaluator exploitation, partner overfitting, and diversity collapse. But we only treat these at the level of desiderata, and do not develop concrete safeguards or protocols for them.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Our paper presents comprehensive survey of coevolution in agentic systems, with specific focus on how agents and their environments adaptively reshape one another, moving from human-designed toward self-directed evolution. All research works reviewed in this survey are properly cited. To the best of our knowledge, the referenced materials are publicly accessible or available under licenses permitting their use for research review. We did not conduct additional dataset curation or human annotation work. Consequently, we believe that this paper does not raise any ethical concerns.

sections.content: Multi-agent interaction. Multiple agents can communicate, collaborate, or compete without changing themselves (Wu et al., 2023; Guo et al., Interaction becomes co-evolution only 2024). when it produces persistent updates to multiple agents and their changes continue to shape one another. Agent loops and loop engineering. An agent loop organizes the repeated steps used to complete task (Xie et al., 2026). Loop engineering designs goals, feedback, verification, and stopping rules of this process. Both concern how tasks are executed rather than whether the agent changes across tasks. Harness engineering. Harness engineering designs the persistent runtime components of an agent, including its prompts, memory, tools, skills, and workflows (Xie et al., 2026). Designing harness alone is not evolution. Evolution occurs only if the model, the harness, or both are updated and retained across runs (Liu et al., 2026i). Even when both change, they still constitute one evolving agent in our definition. Evolutionary optimization. Evolutionary optimization searches over candidate prompts, programs, or agent designs through generation, evaluation, and selection (Chauhan et al., 2025). Its candidates only need to be evaluated and selected, while co-evolution requires persistent adaptive units that change in response to one another. Continual learning. Continual learning repeatedly updates the same learner and preserves its changes as new data or tasks arrive (Parisi et al., 2019). Unlike evolutionary optimization, it accumulates changes within one continuing learner rather than selecting among separate candidates. Its learning procedure can remain fixed, and no other component needs to adapt. Self-play. Self-play is training scheme in which learner interacts with copies or earlier versions of itself (Silver et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2024). It can support self-evolution even when only the current learner changes. In contrast, co-evolution requires multiple adaptive units that retain their changes and continue shaping each other. We retain each surveys original taxonomy and report where co-evolution appears in its organization. Self-evolution. Self-evolution allows an agent to improve while its tasks, feedback rules, counterparts, or other learning conditions remain fixed (Gao et al., 2026). Co-evolution requires another adaptive unit whose changes reshape the agents later evolution while the agent also reshapes that unit. This additional unit may be created by the agent itself, but it must evolve as distinct part during the process. Meta-evolution. Meta-evolution changes the mechanism that governs future evolution, including what, when, how, and where to evolve, and how changes are evaluated (Fernando et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026b). The meta-level controller may remain fixed as long as it modifies this mechanism. Meta Co-Evolution further requires the modification to be driven by and then reshape lower-level co-evolving system. Iterative and recursive self-improvement. Iterative self-improvement repeatedly applies fixed improvement procedure to make system better. Recursive self-improvement also improves this procedure, so the updated system can make more effective self-improvements in later rounds (Schmidhuber, 2007; Chen et al., 2026b). Existing surveys primarily organize the literature around multiagent systems, agent harnesses, self-evolution, recursive improvement, or environment scaling. Coevolution consequently appears as scattered examples, future direction, or one branch of broader taxonomy.
